rv.q: You can't take your eyes off her…You're grateful for every minute you get to spend in the beautiful, miserable company.
This really is, with perhaps one miscalculation, a stunning revival of this churning family exorcism.
This revival of Eugene O'Neill's masterpiece is a thrilling family drama that crackles with emotional intensity.
It’s that attraction to madness that gives this performance such mesmerizing authority.
It is unforgivable, stupid and thoughtless.
Lange maintains close control over the mounting hysteria that will eventually send Mary literally up to the attic and into the past to relive every painful chapter of her history.
Her Mary has a broader emotional palette than any I've seen, including that of Vanessa Redgrave.
This ensemble makes for a compelling evening.
If Kent’s staging is not uniformly absorbing, it’s certainly a creditable effort.
What you do doubt, as you watch them have at one another onstage, is that they are members of the same family, bound by blood ties that will ultimately strangle them.

And that, along with Shannon's unceasing attempts to unlock some of these scenes and spill out their devastating emotional content, is about the only truly successful aspect of this strangely marauding and meandering theatrical experience.
Lacking the ensemble dynamism that makes possible unforeseen discoveries, this O'Neill outing felt like an endless exercise in Beckettian waiting.
This is a Long Day's Journey Into Night that will haunt you long after the final curtain falls, with performances so searing and honest that they seem to burn holes in your heart.
The revival that opened tonight at the Roundabout Theatre Company’s Theatre is, in a word, transfixing.
A magnificent production…Director Jonathan Kent and an extraordinary cast led by Jessica Lange and Gabriel Byrne have achieved a masterful staging of the undisputed classic
The beauty of this production is the perfect balance - both in the writing and performances - that speaks to the emotional interdependence defining so many American families.
Happily, that was the case with my latest visit with the Tyrones at the Roundabout's Theater.

The actors inhabit their characters with as much truth as can be mustered: Lange, for one, seems so immersed that we feel as if we were watching some real Mary Tyrone, and not that marvelous performer we remember from "Frances," or for that matter, “Tootsie.”
This Long Day's Journey Into Night is a production that finds the perfect balance between respecting O'Neill's intentions and making them accessible to contemporary audiences.

But for those who saw the 2003. Broadway production, for example, with Brian Dennehy, Vanessa Redgrave, Philip Seymour Hoffman and Robert Sean Leonard, the new production is likely to feel in some ways disappointing.
Jessica Lange delivers a towering performance as morphine-addicted Mary Tyrone, bringing both fragility and fierce intelligence to O'Neill's tormented matriarch.
The performances here are exceptional all around, but the production is likely to grow smoother and more engrossing as the run continues.
But Shannon and Lange, with a partial victory by Byrne, are not quite enough.
Under Jonathan Kent’s direction, Byrne and Lange handle those sharp changes in tone adeptly to create a mesmerizing dance of death.
O’Neill wrote Long Day’s Journey into Night around 1941, but this might be the first major Broadway production that feels old.
Even a perfectly tuned production can be an endurance test.
Rising to the challenge of the mammoth text (the production runs nearly four hours) is an accomplishment worth celebrating.
Under Jonathan Ken's direction, this show, particularly in the second act, feels more like an excuse for showboat acting than an organic portrait of a family in decline.
This production is crystal clear.
Overall, 'Long Day's Journey Into Night' is a masterpiece which should be seen and will hold your attention throughout the night.

This production of Long Day’s Journey Into Night, under the very tight direction of Jonathan Kent, with an atmospheric set by Tom Pye that allows the New England fog to affect your mood, will send you out into the night after a nourishing and provocative theatrical experience.

"Jessica Lange dominates the production...Actors Gabriel Byrne and John Gallagher Jr’s grip on one scene seemed almost tenuous at times, but that’s the weakest patch in this formidable, searing production. Director Jonathan Kent’s impeccable pacing is most evident in Act 1...Shannon as the older brother perfectly conveys anger’s acid-drip...
This production of Long Day's Journey Into Night is a masterclass in acting, with Jessica Lange delivering a powerhouse performance that anchors the entire evening.
This may or may not be the best version I've seen, but it is certainly the most immediate.
You’ve not truly seen Jessica Lange perform until you catch Roundabout’s revival of Eugene O’Neill’s Long Day’s Journey Into Night— for this is probably her best performance in years, if not ever.
She is mesmerizing, and definitely the reason to see this play, rather than read it.
The actors are committed and Lange effectively captures the woman's isolation, loneliness, and regret.

It’s a memorable performance to put on our collective mental shelf besides her Blanche DuBois in Streetcar Named Desire and her Amanda Wingfield in Glass Menagerie – her only two previous forays on Broadway.
It contributes to an overall tonal incoherence in this production, staged a bit too broadly by Richard Eyre.
I wasn’t moved, not once, either to laughter or tears, during this marathon production of Eugene O’Neill’s posthumous dramatic masterpiece.
Perhaps more fitting as a vintage peep show, than a well executed play, this Long Day’s Journey Into Night, sure makes one crave for the morrow.
